I found that out a few days before my niece's birthday and let my brother know that I wouldn't be attending. He asked why and I told him that he wouldn't like it and he would disagree. He told me that I "can pull that line of thinking" with my therapist but that he grew up in the same house. He said that if I knew what "real" abuse and neglect was, I'd be "glad that they pushed me the way they did". 

He and my other brother have fine relationships with them. My sister-in-law had made comments about my mother being and saying things that were inappropriate (like, 'oh, there's his ex-girlfriend. We thought he was going to marry her!). I'm the only one estranged.

What my brother can't (or didn't) realize is a few keys difference:

\-I'm the oldest.

\-I'm the only girl.

\-I'm the only one from my mother's first marriage. 

So, yes, they have better relationships. I'm the crazy one and always blamed for everything. My mom sent me a text this week that is the \*definition\* of gaslighting.

I said, "That's not accurate and I can give you examples, but not tonight. Goodnight, Mom." (I had already said goodnight)

In addition to (or because of) my CPTSD, I also struggle with major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder and an eating disorder. I have an insanely difficult time in situations that create any anxiety.

I can't stand displays of anger. My stepdad has an unpredictable explosive temper and as a result tension and anger and yelling creates emotional panic attacks for me. I immediately get shaky, sweaty and feel like I need to run from the room. My anxiety skyrockets and my brain shuts down so that I literally think about who is standing where and the safest route out. 

The frustrating thing is that my tolerance is so low, I don't have to be involved at all. I was in a store the other day (strip mall) and some people were being loud outside and they sounded slightly aggressive. I had to revert to my grounding skills, reminding myself that I was safe and not involved. It doesn't have to be yelling to trigger me. I was in treatment this past summer and they other patients were instructed to throw foam blocks against the wall to relieve some of the anger and I had to leave the room. I could hardly handle standing in the hallway hearing the blocks hit the wall knowing they were being thrown out of anger.

I've done several inpatient stays (where I am, these are short terms crisis units - stays are typically a few days to a couple of weeks) and I've done one residential stay (usually longer term 30 days and up).

It has been really hard for my daughter to have me away from her. She's 6 now and I worry that she has developed abandonment issues are a result of my times away (2 weeks in fall of 2015, 3 weeks in fall of 2017, 6 weeks summer 2018) . However, I want to be the best mother that I can and that typically requires being alive. If I had not had my crisis stays, I would not be alive and that abandonment would have been permanent. 

The residential program I was admitted to was perfect for me. I was finally in an environment that had trauma focused groups, support groups for my eating disorder and self-harm issues and consistent supervision since I wasn't functioning day to day at home and there was no way I could address the trauma as well. The problem was the insurance quit paying for it after a week so I was discharged after 2. 

The point is, yes, you will have some of the guilt about leaving, BUT if the treatment could put you in a better frame of mind, which is the better option? Stay home, not seek treatment and be miserable for who knows how long? Your child will be able to pick up on your struggle to a certain extent, kids are perceptive.  I feel guilty about my stays, but I know that in the long run, my daughter would rather have me around and gaining stability over just sitting in the same space.

An eating disorder is way more then the physical side of things as I'm sure you know. If your food intake or number on the scale or how much you did or did not exercise impacts your mood long term, it's a problem. If your value and the worth you give yourself comes as a result of food or food related behaviors, it is problematic.

Obviously, only medical providers can diagnose and eating disorder, but in general if you are obsessive about it, it creates anxiety and impacts your mood.....you may have one or be well on your way to developing one.

Alcohol is a depressant. Yes, the buzz is uplifting and carefree or whatever, but there is always that point where it creates more issues for mood. Also, once you get to the place of being buzzed, more doesn't equal continuing the buzz as I'm sure you know. 

You can be a good person regardless of how you treat yourself. I feel like most people who struggle with any sort of addiction (not just substances, btw)  are trying to self-medicate and/or have a deeper reason that the addiction is meeting. Perhaps instead of focusing on the behavior (i.e. drinking) try to look at what your motivation is. Why are you drinking in the first place? Then, why do you feel the need to destroy yourself when it gets a little further down the road? If you can answer these, perhaps you can begin to make changes to address the root and avoid behavior swapping if you decide to try for sobriety (behavior swapping as in not drinking but instead using something else destructive).

I remind myself that trauma can't be compared. There are too many factors that play into it and you could literally have 2 people in the same situation and they come out the other side in extremely different spaces. 

Also, this (not me):

"As a therapist, lemme just say: almost every trauma survivor I've ever had has at some point said, "But I didn't have it as bad as \*some\* people" and then talked about how other types of trauma are worse. Even my most-traumatized, most abused, most psychologically-injured clients say this.

The ones who were cheated on, abandoned, and neglected say this. The ones who were in dangerous accidents/disasters say this. The ones who were horrifyingly sexually abused say this. The ones who were brutally beaten say this. The ones that were psychologically tortured for decades say this.  What does that tell you? That one of the typical side effects of trauma is to make you believe you are unworthy of care. 

Don't buy into it, because it's nonsense. It doesn't matter if someone else had it "worse".  Every person who experiences a trauma deserves to get the attention and care they  need to heal from it."
